reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Characterised by proximal interphalangeal joint flexion combined with distal interphalangeal joint hyperextension
The primary lesion is disruption of the central slip at its insertion on the dorsal base of the middle phalanx
As the central slip fails, the lateral bands migrate volar to the axis of the proximal interphalangeal joint so that they flex it and hyperextend the distal joint
The Elson test detects an acute central slip injury, showing weak proximal interphalangeal extension and a rigid distal joint when the joint is flexed over an edge
Common causes include forced flexion of an extended finger, volar dislocation, dorsal laceration, and attritional rupture in rheumatoid arthritis
The deformity characteristically develops over the days following injury rather than appearing immediately
It must be distinguished from a pseudo-boutonniere, in which a volar plate injury causes a proximal interphalangeal flexion contracture without distal joint hyperextension

Generic management is proximal interphalangeal extension splinting with the distal joint left free for closed acute injuries, and surgery for displaced avulsions, open injuries or established deformity
reference.pathophysiology: A boutonniere deformity develops when the central slip insertion at the dorsal base of the middle phalanx is disrupted, removing the principal extensor of the proximal interphalangeal joint. The triangular ligament that normally tethers the lateral bands dorsally becomes attenuated, allowing the lateral bands to subluxate volar to the joint axis. In this displaced position the lateral bands act as flexors of the proximal interphalangeal joint and hyperextensors of the distal interphalangeal joint, and progressive contracture fixes the posture. In rheumatoid arthritis the same imbalance is produced by synovitis-driven attenuation of the extensor mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-boutonniere from a volar plate hyperextension injury
Dupuytren contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint
Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthropathy with digital deformity
A locked trigger finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint
additionalInvestigations: The Elson test to identify an acute central slip injury before the deformity is fully established
Plain radiographs to detect a dorsal avulsion fragment and assess the joint
Serial clinical assessment to detect an evolving deformity
Ultrasound or MRI to evaluate the central slip when the diagnosis is unclear
Screening for an inflammatory arthropathy when the deformity is atraumatic
redFlags: An open laceration over the proximal interphalangeal joint involving the extensor mechanism and joint
A fixed established contracture that limits treatment options
reference.prognosis: Early recognition and splinting give good results, whereas an established fixed deformity is difficult to correct and the outcomes of reconstructive surgery are less predictable.
pitfalls: Missing the acute central slip injury because the deformity is delayed, which the Elson test helps avoid
Confusing the deformity with a pseudo-boutonniere and mismanaging it
Unnecessarily splinting the distal interphalangeal joint
Under-recognising rheumatoid arthritis as the underlying cause
management: Splinting the proximal interphalangeal joint in full extension while leaving the distal interphalangeal joint free, for acute closed central slip injuries
Hand therapy with active and passive exercises to preserve distal interphalangeal and proximal interphalangeal mobility and prevent contracture
Operative repair or reinsertion of the central slip for open injuries or a displaced dorsal avulsion fragment
Disease-modifying antirheumatic therapy to control synovitis when the deformity is attritional in rheumatoid arthritis
Serial clinical review with the Elson test to detect an evolving deformity before it becomes fixed
Reconstructive surgery such as lateral band relocation or tendon reconstruction for an established fixed deformity
Referral to hand surgery for chronic, complex or rotationally significant injuries
